latin: Sicut Apollo est intellectus solaris, ita Aesculapius est intellectus lunaris.
translation: Just as Apollo is the solar intellect, so Aesculapius is the lunar intellect.
translation_note: Compare Busi and Ebgi's own Italian rendering of the same thesis, 'Come Apollo è l'intelletto solare, cosi Asclepio è l'intelletto lunare' (busi2014:7251), which independently supports this reading.
translator: original translation, drafted 2026-09-26 by WRITER-full-batch9, from Latin at farmer1998:15459

sources.pico_relation: Farmer identifies this Proclus passage, which sets Porphyry against Iamblichus, as the source for theses 22.4-8

doctrine: Farmer places the thesis in a set (22.4-8) adapted from Proclus's Timaeus commentary that pits Porphyry's reading against Iamblichus's, the first of a series of theses involving astrological correspondences that Farmer stresses do not endorse the horoscopic astrology Pico attacks elsewhere (farmer1998:15531). Farmer glosses 'Apollo'/solar intellect as Pico's 'total' or 'angelic' intellect, and 'Aesculapius'/lunar intellect as the passive intellect or reason, comparing thesis 5>19 (farmer1998:15531).
context: Busi and Ebgi likewise trace the thesis to Proclus's commentary on the Timaeus, reading it as Pico's Porphyrian identification of Apollo with the solar intellect (busi2014:7251).
historiography: Busi and Ebgi (2014) cite the thesis, in a discussion of the Oration's Apolline solar symbolism, as evidence of Pico's derivation of the Apollo/solar-intellect identification from Proclus (busi2014:7251).
not_established: Whether Busi and Ebgi's citation of Proclus, In Timaeum (Diehl 1:159) names the same passage as Farmer's citation (Diehl 1:147, 159) is not further specified in the material consulted.
Pico's own considered view, beyond reporting Porphyry, is not established by the sources consulted.
